AdapterActionResponse.description:
Shared response shape for adapter passthrough action endpoints.

Used by every action that fires a write at the controller and
returns a small ack-shaped dict (toggle port, PoE control, port
profile apply, LAG CRUD, etc.). The shape mirrors the
``AdapterResult`` dataclass returned by the adapter layer:

- ``success``: True when the adapter accepted the write
- ``message``: human-readable description (e.g. ``"PoE enabled"``)
- ``data``: free-form passthrough from the adapter for the
  specific operation (keys vary by vendor and operation)
- ``error``: present only when ``success=False`` — vendor error text

This is INTENTIONALLY a thin envelope. We don't try to lock down
the vendor-specific ``data`` keys here because each adapter
returns different fields per operation, and forcing a schema
would force every vendor to a lowest-common-denominator dict.
The envelope gives the OpenAPI generator (and TypeScript
consumers) something to bind against while keeping the
per-vendor flexibility we need.
AdapterActionResponse.title: AdapterActionResponse

BrowserAuthResponse.description:
Slim auth response for browser cookie-based endpoints.

The browser already receives access + refresh tokens via httpOnly cookies
set in the ``Set-Cookie`` response header.  Echoing the raw token values
in the JSON body is unnecessary and exposes them to JavaScript (XSS risk).

the JSON body carries no bearer-usable secrets.

A ``response_model`` is a WHITELIST: FastAPI validates the endpoint's
return value against it and drops every key this class does not declare,
silently and with a 200. So an endpoint cannot signal anything from here
that is not a field above -- the frontend read
``data.force_password_change`` for three releases and got ``undefined``
every time, because nothing declared it. Add the field before you send it.

MfaChallengeResponse.description:
The OTHER 200 shape of ``POST /auth/login``: MFA is required.

``/auth/login`` was declared ``response_model=BrowserAuthResponse`` when the
raw tokens were taken out of the body, but its MFA branch returns
``{"require_mfa": True, "mfa_token": ...}`` -- which has none of that
model's required ``expires_in``. FastAPI validates the return value against
the response model, so that branch raised ResponseValidationError and every
MFA-enabled user got a 500 from /auth/login instead of a challenge, unable
to sign in at all. It went unnoticed because every test calls the ``login``
coroutine directly, and calling the function bypasses the response model.

Declared as a separate model rather than as optional fields on
``BrowserAuthResponse`` so neither shape can be returned half-filled: the
success body must carry ``expires_in``, the challenge body must carry a
token, and ``/auth/refresh`` and ``/auth/login/mfa`` keep the narrow model.

require_mfa.description: True when the credentials were correct but MFA is due

RefreshTokenRequest.description:
Token refresh request.

``refresh_token`` is OPTIONAL because the endpoint documents itself as
accepting "refresh token from JSON body OR httpOnly cookie" -- a browser
has the cookie and has nothing to put in the body.

It used to be required, and that made the whole refresh path unusable from
the SPA. The axios interceptor posts ``{}`` (client.ts) and the auth store
posts ``{}`` (authStore.ts), which is a PRESENT body that failed
validation, so every refresh returned 422. The interceptor treats that as
a failed refresh, clears auth state and drops the user on the login screen.

Net effect: the access token lives 3600s, and at expiry the very mechanism
meant to renew the session silently ended it instead. Sessions could never
outlive one token lifetime. Found by driving the live UI -- the suite never
posts an empty body, and ``curl`` with no body at all returns 200, so both
of the obvious checks pass.
RefreshTokenRequest.title: RefreshTokenRequest

post.description:
Verify agent credentials (agent_id + agent_key).

NOTE: previously this endpoint returned three distinct
failure shapes — bad UUID format, valid creds but ``is_enabled=False``,
not-approved, and invalid creds. An attacker holding only a leaked
agent_id could probe to learn whether the agent existed and whether it
was enabled, which is useful intel for targeted social-engineering of
the site operator (e.g. "your agent X is offline — please enable it").
All failure cases now collapse to a single
``{"valid": false, "message": "Invalid credentials"}`` response and the
real reason is logged server-side at WARNING for ops triage.
Mark agents as offline if they haven't sent a heartbeat recently.

Requires an authenticated, unscoped platform superuser. ``valid`` alone

``state_authenticated``, ``boundary_verified`` and

serialized window budget. ``next_start_id`` points to the first unexamined
row, but subsequent requests use new snapshots. Missing/reversed bounds or
detected inconsistencies produce ``valid: false``.

of deleted bodies. ``history_authenticated`` and
``external_immutability_proven`` remain false: this endpoint cannot prove
complete event capture, external immutability or whole-database rollback
resistance. A valid unsigned/unsealed result is not a certification.

UI. Returns metadata only — never the raw refresh token / JTI.

"Active" is now enforced, not just claimed. This selected every
``user_sessions`` row the user had ever produced, with no bound: a session
from six months ago whose refresh token died in week two came back looking
exactly like the laptop the user is holding, and the only deleter of those
rows (``cleanup_orphan_sessions``) had no beat entry, so nothing ever
trimmed them. 135 rows for the fleet on the dev DB, none prunable.

A row is listed only while the refresh token bound to it could still be
presented:

* ``expires_at`` is that token's own expiry, stamped by ``_upsert_session``;
  once it is past, both tokens on the row are dead.
* Rows written before that column was populated carry NULL. ``last_used_at``
  is re-stamped on every refresh, so ``last activity + the longest refresh
  window`` is an upper bound on when their token dies. ``created_at`` is the
  floor for rows that were never refreshed (NULL ``last_used_at``).

Revoked rows that are still inside that window ARE listed, and carry
``is_revoked``/``revoked_at`` so the UI can show "signed out on this
device" — they are also exactly the rows whose existence is what keeps a
revoked refresh token rejected (``session_revocation`` treats a MISSING row
as not-revoked), so hiding them would hide the enforcement.

Clients should use this instead of embedding the long-lived access token in query parameters, mitigating **C5 (JWT tokens exposed in URL query parameters)**. This is the chokepoint for all token-authenticated media (snapshot, MJPEG, fMP4, HLS, playback-frame): enforcing the per-camera ``live`` grant here means a user without access to this camera can never mint a media token for it, so the downstream media endpoints inherit the restriction.

get.description: Proxy an MJPEG stream from a Hikvision camera/NVR channel. Scales to 64+ concurrent channels via adaptive frame-rate: - ≤8 streams → 10 fps - ≤16 streams → 5 fps - ≤32 streams → 3 fps - ≤64 streams → 2 fps - >64 streams → 1 fps Pass ``max_fps`` to override the auto-scaling cap. the previous version accepted long-lived access tokens via ``?token=`` which then leaked into nginx access logs, browser history, and Referer headers. The fix: * If cookie auth is present (browser session), it is the PRIMARY credential — prefer it and ignore any redundant ``?token=``. A same-origin ```` always attaches the cookie, and the FE also appends a short-lived stream token (the legacy auth path for tags that can't set headers), so cookie+token arriving together is the *normal* browser case, not an attack. The cookie still outranks the token, so a leaked URL can't bypass or downgrade cookie auth. * Otherwise accept ``?token=`` ONLY when it's a stream-scoped token (60s TTL) issued via ``/stream-token``. Bearer header remains a first-class auth path for clients that can set it.

The pending-changes drawer used to fire one HTTP request per

drilldown views that DO want only one domain).

get.description:
Kubernetes / load-balancer readiness probe.

HARD-gates (503) on what makes THIS instance unable to serve: the per-instance
primary DB connection and critical subsystems (event_bus, modules). Redis and
LogDB are PROBED and REPORTED in the payload but do NOT gate by default —
they are SHARED dependencies, so hard-gating readiness on them would make a
transient Redis blip (or the ~9s Sentinel failover window) pull EVERY instance
out of the LB at once → a cascading full outage. Set READINESS_STRICT_DEPS=true
to also 503 on Redis/LogDB.

Uses fresh, time-boxed connections (NOT the pooled request session) so a
frozen DB fails fast at 503 instead of hanging — see _probe_db_engine.

delete.description:
Uninstall a plugin (calls on_uninstall hook then removes files).

Settings are KEPT by default and a reinstall picks them back up, which is
what makes uninstall-reinstall a safe troubleshooting step. The cost is that
a credential outlives the plugin that used it, and the uninstall dialog used
to say only that settings "may remain" -- vague about something that always
happens, and silent about the part that matters, which is the token.

``purge_settings=true`` removes them. Kept as a choice rather than made the
default because the two reasons to uninstall want opposite behaviour: fixing
a misbehaving plugin wants the configuration back, and removing a plugin you
are done with wants the credential gone.

get.description:
HTTP provisioning endpoint — phones request their config here.

Grandstream phones will request: ``GET /voip/provisioning/cfg{MAC}.xml``

SECURITY: this endpoint was previously unauthenticated and
returned config for ANY MAC. Anyone who knew or guessed a MAC could
pull SIP credentials (P34) and admin web passwords (P2) for any
tenant. We now require BOTH:

  1. The MAC must resolve to a known Phone row — the tenant is
     derived from that row's site, NEVER from request input.
  2. The source IP must be inside one of the site's configured
     subnets, OR the URL must carry a valid HMAC signature
     (``?sig=<hex>``) generated from the same MAC + the server's
     encryption key.

Returns 404 on any failure so an attacker can't distinguish
"MAC doesn't exist" from "MAC exists but you're not authorised".

get.description:
Voicemail audio download — NOT YET AVAILABLE.

``VoicemailMessage.file_path`` holds the recording's spool path on
the *remote PBX* host (e.g. ``/var/spool/asterisk/voicemail/.../msg0000.wav``).
FreeSDN runs as a separate service and has no filesystem access to
that path, and no FreePBX/Asterisk adapter method exposes the
recording bytes over its API (the REST/AJAX client explicitly
returns nothing for voicemail; ARI only serves call recordings, not
mailbox messages). So there is currently NO safe, read-only way to
retrieve the audio.

This previously returned ``file_path`` as if it were downloadable,
which let the UI hand the user a dead server-side path. We now fail
honestly with 501 rather than leak the spool path. The org-scoped
lookup is still performed first so this can't be used to probe
whether a voicemail ID exists in another tenant (404 wins over 501).

To implement real downloads later: add a read-only adapter method to
fetch the recording bytes (e.g. AMI ``VoicemailRefresh`` + a sound
file fetch, or an out-of-band SCP/agent on the PBX), then stream them
here with the correct ``audio/wav`` media type. Until then the FE
keeps the Download button disabled with an explanatory tooltip.
